Compares three-season rotations using NA: Compares three-season rotations using NASA weather history, farmer-entered soil and irrigation, a small crop table, and adjustable priorities. This prototype follows a Southern Karnataka June–September / October–January / February–May calendar. Coordinates work globally, but this crop calendar and crop list are not calibrated for other regions.
Daily NASA POWER historical estimates ar: Daily NASA POWER historical estimates are requested for {{n0}} Jan {{n1}}–{{n2}} Dec {{n3}}. Fill values (including {{n4}}) are treated as missing, never as rain or temperature. Only complete calendar years enter annual charts. Only complete June–May cycles enter the replay: a complete {{n5}}-calendar-year file therefore yields {{n6}} rotation cycles. A dry day has less than {{n7}} mm rain; a very hot day exceeds {{n8}}°C. Trends are ordinary least squares, reported per decade.
Indicative crop water demand is the midp: Indicative crop water demand is the midpoint of the table range. The crop starts on the first day of its planning season; only rain during its assumed growth duration counts. Captured rain is {{n0}}% for sandy soil, {{n1}}% for loam and {{n2}}% for clay, plus {{n3}} / {{n4}} / {{n5}} mm of selected irrigation. These are illustrative capture assumptions, not a measured soil-water balance. There is no water storage between seasons, irrigation efficiency model, runoff routing, or daily stress model. Water fit is min({{n6}} supply ÷ demand × {{n7}}), averaged across seasons and complete cycles. Fallow has zero crop demand and a water score of {{n8}}.
The rainfall slider scales daily rain by: The rainfall slider scales daily rain by {{n0}}% to {{n1}}%. Temperature adds {{n2}}–{{n3}}°C to mean and maximum air temperature. Crop water demand rises by an illustrative {{n4}}% per added °C. The model recomputes water and climate fit against the adjusted historical days. This is a sensitivity test, not a downscaled climate projection.
{{n0}} minus {{n1}} points per °C outsid: {{n0}} minus {{n1}} points per °C outside the assumed mean-temperature range and {{n2}} times the fraction of growth-window days above the crop’s upper temperature bound, clipped to {{n3}}–{{n4}}.
starts at {{n0}} adds {{n1}} for a legum: starts at {{n0}} adds {{n1}} for a legume and {{n2}} per distinct cropped family; subtracts {{n3}} for each adjacent same-family pair (including the year boundary), {{n4}} per duplicate crop, average pH distance × {{n5}} and {{n6}} per crop with a nonpreferred soil texture (averaged).
duration-weighted assumed crop cover wit: duration-weighted assumed crop cover with {{n0}}/{{n1}} cover after harvest; retained-residue fallow scores {{n2}}. This is a cover proxy, not a measured erosion rate.
an illustrative relative index, not pric: an illustrative relative index, not prices, profit or yield.
All season-eligible combinations from {{: All season-eligible combinations from {{n0}} crops plus fallow are scored. Three identical crops and more than one fallow season are excluded from alternatives. The baseline is always shown even if it breaks those assumptions. The priorities plan retains the highest weighted score. Next, water, soil and weather plans are selected in that order from unique candidates. Each prefers at least two changed season slots from every already selected plan, including the baseline; if none exists, uniqueness alone is used and the relaxation is disclosed. Water ranks by water fit then lower demand; soil by the soil score then cover; weather by temperature fit then covered historical cycles and lower mean deficit. Diversity can reduce a category score. Rest seasons score {{n1}} for water and temperature fit because no crop is exposed; this is not evidence of a more productive farm. Farmer weights map to water, soil, income, and the average of climate and cover. All-zero weights fall back to equal weights across the five components. “Highest” always refers to this model and candidate set.
